chapters.narrative: Guatemala revealed itself in layers—first the raw power of its living mountains, then the quiet life nestled in their shadow. events.title: Participated in the elementary school speech competition
events.detail: A teacher advised me not to sing. That was the first time I learned I was probably tone-deaf.

learning.text: A teacher told me I couldn't sing, and I think I still might be tone deaf to this day. I have remembered that sentence for twenty years, which probably says more about how long an offhand remark from a teacher lasts than it does about my voice.

events.title: Started at Stuyvesant
events.detail: Surrounded by the brightest of NYC.

learning.text: Being surrounded by people who are genuinely exceptional at one thing is humbling, and the wrong lesson to take from it is to go find your one thing and grind. The right one — the one it took me years to act on — is that you need to be good at more than one thing to excel. The overlap is where you're actually rare.

events.title: Graduated Stuyvesant
events.detail: Four years at Stuyvesant, then a year at Stony Brook to earn the transfer.

events.title: Stony Brook University
events.detail: The year between. Head down on the requirement classes and the GPA needed to secure the guaranteed transfer to Cornell.

events.title: Family trip to visit home, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Thailand
events.detail: First family trip — learned to tolerate each other more, and began to enjoy travelling the world.

events.title: Cornell, on a guaranteed transfer
events.detail: September 2018. B.S. Information Science. Joined clubs and organizations; made lifelong connections.

learning.text: Stuyvesant taught me there were more talented people than I'd assumed. Cornell taught me the same lesson one level up — more intelligent, harder-working, and no end to it. At some point you stop measuring yourself against the room and start looking for the people you want to keep.

events.title: Collegiate table tennis
events.detail: Played on the team. If only college pickleball had been a thing back then.

events.title: Lockdown, alone on campus
events.detail: The lockdown came out of nowhere. I stayed at Cornell because it was safer than home in NYC, and had the whole campus to myself.

learning.text: I had an empty Cornell campus to myself for months and almost no record of it. I wish I had taken the photos and flown the drone. What I did find was running, which I still have — so the year wasn't empty, it just left less behind than it should have. Document the strange stretches while you are inside them.

events.title: Moved to Seattle
events.detail: June 2021, for a job at Amazon. Started in inbound sales.

learning.text: Moving across the country to a city where I knew almost no one is the thing I would have called the risky choice at the time. It is where I got comfortable in my own skin, professionally and otherwise. The confidence did not come from the job — it came from having to build a life from nothing in particular.

eras.label: Island kid, radio voice, chess board
eras.note: Born on the island, announced the weather on kindergarten radio, got told not to sing, and started playing chess in tournaments.
eras.why: These years are the only ones lived entirely in Hainan, and the record is a handful of small, scattered milestones (2002 radio, 2004 speech competition, 2005 chess) with no photos or video. The era ends where the 2006 entries begin, when the person tells a teacher they are going to America.

eras.label: Dropped a grade, found the ping pong table
eras.note: The family moved to New York, he was put back a grade for lack of English, then became a top junior ping pong prospect and appeared in a Times Square Wii campaign.
eras.why: The 2006 move is the emotional center. It is the only event he wrote about twice, in the 2016 poem and again in 2026, with the line about his dad's tear. Everything through 2012 (the grade drop, ping pong in 2009, Wii Sports in Times Square) is the aftermath of arriving and finding a footing, before Stuyvesant changes the setting.

eras.label: Stuyvesant to Cornell: always the room above me
eras.place: New York City, Stony Brook, Ithaca
eras.note: Stuyvesant, a transfer-securing year at Stony Brook, Cornell in Information Science, collegiate table tennis, and the empty-campus lockdown.
eras.why: His own reflections on Stuyvesant and Cornell make the same point (more talented people than he'd assumed, then the same lesson one level up), so these years read as one long stretch of measuring himself against stronger rooms. The 2020 lockdown, which he says left almost no record, closes it as a visible gap in what was documented, just before the Seattle move.

eras.label: Seattle, building a life from nothing in particular
eras.note: Moved across the country for Amazon, worked in inbound sales and then AWS games and betting, switched to Program Manager in March 2024, and began traveling.
eras.why: The June 2021 move is where he places his confidence ('came from having to build a life from nothing'). The career change in 2024 is the other event he reflects on. Photos first appear in 2023 and thicken in 2024 (Panama, Angkor Wat, Chicago, sailing), so the record changes here from milestones to lived texture.

eras.label: Competing at 5.0, and out the door every weekend
eras.note: Entered pickleball tournaments, built a community, built Stacked, traveled (Guatemala, Japan and Taiwan, Costa Rica, Kauai), explored the Cascades and Oregon Coast, and made Remnant.
eras.why: This is by far the densest stretch in the record: a dozen photos in 2025, a dozen more plus a video in 2026, and four chapters. It starts in January 2025 with competitive pickleball, which he credits with giving him a community, and it runs through the present, where the record is being made.

achievements.title: Inbound sales → AWS, games and betting
achievements.detail: Started in inbound sales at Amazon, moved to AWS selling into the games industry, then into betting and gaming specifically. Through 2024.
achievements.why: This leaves out the sales career: three years in inbound sales and AWS games and betting, which looks impressive from outside. He never draws a lesson from it. When he talks about those years, he credits the Seattle move and not the job for his confidence.

achievements.title: Program Manager — Amazon Business
achievements.detail: March 2024. A new role, a new foundation, a different skillset from sales.

learning.text: Changing discipline three years in means being a beginner again on purpose, in front of people who watched you be competent at something else. That trade is almost always worth it, and it never once feels like it in the first six months.

achievements.why: He wrote a real lesson on this one: changing discipline means being a beginner on purpose, and the trade is worth it even though it doesn't feel that way at first. A pivot he reflects on this honestly counts for more than the longer sales stretch he only lists.

achievements.title: Competing at 5.0
achievements.detail: January 2025 — started playing pickleball tournaments competitively. Won a few local ones. Met a lot of people along the way and built a community.

learning.text: I went in for the competition and what I actually got was a community. The tournaments are the excuse; the people you keep showing up with are the thing. If you are deciding whether to enter — enter, and not for the result.

achievements.why: He returns to it in his own words with a clear point: the tournaments are the excuse and the community is the thing, so enter and don't do it for the result. That is a lesson aimed at the reader, and it anchors his most recent and most documented era.

quotes.text: In first grade I told my teacher I was going to America, a decision I couldn't quite understand.
Forty thousand feet above ground, I pondered on the cold seat as I leaned on mom's shoulder. I knew she was excited. But I was afraid.
That was the first time I saw dad let down a tear. I knew he was worried about me. But in that moment, I also knew that he was scared of this place just like I was.
